newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: FOCUS-Fight for Slovak crown could hurt economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Fight for Slovak crown could hurt economy.

text.p: The Slovak central bank kept up its support for its currency on Thursday in a battle against speculative selling, but analysts said the fight for the crown could be costly for the economy if it goes on for long.
High interest rates, resulting from a liquidity squeeze by the National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) to discourage banks from short-selling the crown, could hurt companies and hinder economic growth.

"It will take around two weeks for the economy outside the financial market to start feeling the negative effect of high interbank rates," added Martin Barto of ING Barings. "Then the economic growth will be in danger," he said.
The Slovak and Czech crowns have for the past week been under strong speculative pressure, mainly from foreign banks.
The Czech and Slovak economies, and their currencies, remained closely linked after Czechoslovakia peacefully split into the Czech and Slovak republics in 1993.

While the Czech National Bank (CNB) has intervened several times on the market to boost the ailing currency this week, the National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) has used only indirect intervention through its regular fixing.
The NBS fixed the crown at -0.78 percent against its mark/dollar basket parity on Thursday, a level it has been fixing it since last Monday.
The crown was trading at around -1.46 percent before Thursday's fixing after it had tested -2.00 percent levels earlier in the day.
The more volatile Czech crown slumped to a new low of six percent below parity on Thursday before regaining ground.
Many economists say a devaluation of the Czech crown is inevitable and Slovak analysts say that, as the Czechs' main trading partner, it would be difficult for Slovakia to resist following suit.

"Even though our macroeconomic problems, such as the trade deficit, do not seem as hot as the Czech ones, we would have to follow them if they devalue their curency by more than 10 percent," Vladimir Kuklis of CSOB bank said.
Traders said the NBS's stronger fixing and what they called its wise strategy of keeping liquidity tight on the local money market had so far prevented the crown from more radical decline.
But analysts warned the NBS battle against downward pessure, if it goes on for long, could seriously hurt the currency's image, endanger the country's economy and spark inflationary pressures.
Slovak banks together lacked some six billion crowns as of Thursday to meet minimum reserves requirements.
Short-term rates on the interbank market jumped to a record 44 percent on Thursday morning and local banks stopped quoting crown rates due to an acute liquidity shortage on the market.

"I think the NBS wants to use its market tools to push local commercial banks to stop lending crowns and selling hard currencies to foreign banks so that it should not have to impose any administrative measures," said Martin Hrozany of Credit Lyonnais Bank.

But Hrozany added that if Slovak commercial banks stop trading crowns with foreign banks, as they stopped quoted depo rates on the money market earlier on Thursday, it could seriously hurt the crown's image.
"Furthermore, high money market rates can be dangerous for the economy if sustained for a longer period," Hrozany said.
Even large Slovak companies often turn to short-term loans to refinance thier activities and high rates can make their production more expensive.
"If the rates remain so high, companies will have to add the cost of the funds to their prices and this will bring inflationary presssure," Hrozany said.
-- Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-521-8402
